The primitives describe a triadic temporal structure in receptor response: latency, recruitment, and decay. Recruitment is governed by stimulus energy and rate, modeled as a product of energy and inverse time. This leads to an exponential rise in discharge frequency, bounded by physical limits. Post-peak, decay follows a negative exponential, reflecting adaptation. The after-discharge introduces a non-linear temporal extension, dependent on central propagation. These operators form a closed-loop system where each phase influences the next through feedback mechanisms. Temporal duality emerges: rapid recruitment vs. slow decay, with after-discharge bridging states. Failure modes include saturation during recruitment and premature decay due to stimulus interruption. The system exhibits robustness under constant stimuli but instability when interrupted. Mathematical consistency requires boundedness of all variables and monotonicity of decay. The interplay between these operators enables predictive modeling of sensory behavior across domains.
